belizean-rum: Sugarcane and rum were part of life in Belize through its years as British Honduras, but the modern Belizean rum story belongs to one family business. In 1953 the Perdomo family opened a small bar called Travellers on the edge of Belize City and began blending rum to sell over its counter. The bar grew into Travellers Liquors, the country's leading rum house, and One Barrel, its aged blend, became the Belizean rum most visitors know.
rum-popo: Rum popo is Belize's Christmas drink, a household mix of rum, condensed or evaporated milk, egg and nutmeg, made to share with visitors through the season. It belongs to the family of eggy holiday drinks that runs from Mexico's rompope to Puerto Rico's coquito, and the name looks like a cousin of rompope, though nobody has recorded how it came about. No one is credited with inventing it, and every family recipe differs a little. Bottled versions have since carried it onto shop shelves.
ron-ligero: The light Cuban style is usually dated to 1862, when Facundo Bacardí Massó, a Catalan merchant in Santiago de Cuba, bought a small distillery with his brother José. His work with selected yeast, charcoal filtration and ageing in oak gave a rum soft enough to drink young and mix freely, and other Cuban houses followed the same path. The Bacardí family left the island after the revolution, but the ligero style stayed, and Cuban producers still age even their white rums in oak before filtering them back to clarity.
rhum-barbancourt: Rhum Barbancourt was founded in Haiti in 1862 by Dupré Barbancourt, a Frenchman from the Charente, who applied his home region's double distillation, the method behind cognac, to Haitian cane juice; the house still works that way. He and his wife, Nathalie Gardère, had no children, so the business passed to her nephew Paul Gardère and has stayed in the Gardère family since. Paul's son Jean later moved the distillery to the Domaine Barbancourt near Damien, on the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac.
mamajuana: Mamajuana's roots are usually traced to the Taíno, who steeped barks, roots and herbs, with Spanish settlers later adding wine and then rum. The name comes from damajuana, the Spanish word for a demijohn, the big wicker-covered bottle the mixture was kept in, itself from the French dame-jeanne. In the mid twentieth century Jesús Rodríguez of San Juan de la Maguana is credited with popularising it, and the story goes that under Trujillo its sale was restricted to people with a medical licence.
barbados-rum: Barbados has a strong claim to rum's beginnings. By the 1650s the island's sugar planters were distilling the by-products of cane into a fierce spirit, and a description of the island from that decade calls it rumbullion and kill-devil, the likely root of the word rum. Mount Gay traces itself to a deed of 1703 for an estate in the parish of St Lucy, the basis of its claim to be the oldest rum brand still made. The name honours Sir John Gay Alleyne, who managed the estate.
trinidad-rum: Rum on Trinidad grew up with the island's sugar estates under Spanish and then British rule, and for much of the twentieth century several distilleries worked there. The industry consolidated over time: the state-owned Caroni distillery, now prized by collectors for its heavy rums, closed when the national sugar company was wound down, leaving the Angostura works in Laventille as the island's main producer. Angostura is better known for its bitters, named after the Venezuelan town where they were first made.
angostura-bitters: Angostura bitters began in 1824 in the Venezuelan town of Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar, where Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German surgeon serving in Simón Bolívar's army, compounded them as a tonic for the troops. They took the town's name and contain no bark of the angostura tree. After Siegert's death his sons moved the business to Port of Spain, Trinidad, in 1875. The company says the oversized label came from two brothers who redesigned bottle and label separately, and that a competition judge persuaded them to keep it.
shrubb: Shrubb is a Christmas tradition of the French Antilles, made in Martinique and Guadeloupe by steeping rhum with dried orange peel, sugar and spice. Nobody is credited with inventing it; it began as a household preparation for the festive season, with each family keeping its own recipe. The name is generally traced to the English shrub, a family of cordials built from fruit and spirit that was common across the colonial Caribbean. Agricole houses such as Clément later bottled their own versions, carrying it beyond the holidays.
black-seal-rum: Gosling's began in 1806, when James Gosling, son of a London wine merchant, was bound for Virginia with a cargo of wines and spirits; the story goes that his ship's charter ran out and he landed in Bermuda instead. He opened a shop on the island, and around 1860 the family began blending rum. The firm later filled champagne bottles from the officers' messes of the Bermuda garrison and sealed them with black wax, and customers asking for the black seal rum gave it its name.
rivers-royale: Rivers rum comes from the River Antoine estate in St Patrick, on Grenada's north-east coast, where the distillery has worked since 1785. The estate's cane is still crushed by a water-driven wheel, and the juice is fermented and distilled much in the old way, which is why River Antoine is widely called the oldest functioning water-powered distillery in the Caribbean. The rum, sold as Rivers and Rivers Royale, takes its name from the estate, and most of it never leaves Grenada.
nutmeg-liqueur: Grenada's nutmeg liqueurs follow the spice itself. Nutmeg is native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, and the usual account credits Frank Gurney with planting Grenada's first trees in the mid nineteenth century. The crop took so well that the island became known as the Spice Isle and put a nutmeg on its flag at independence. Local makers steep the nut and the red mace that wraps it in rum or spirit and sweeten the result; no single producer is credited with the first bottle.
saint-lucian-rum: Modern Saint Lucian rum starts in 1931, when Denis Barnard built a distillery at Dennery on the island's east coast. In 1972 the Barnards joined the Geest company, which ran the only other working distillery, at Roseau, to form Saint Lucia Distillers; their first joint rum, Denros, took its name from the two sites. The company, known for Chairman's Reserve, now makes its rums at Roseau in both a column still and copper pot stills, an unusually varied set-up for one Caribbean distillery.
english-harbour-rum: Antigua Distillery was founded in 1932 by a group of merchants and rum shop owners, many of Portuguese descent, who pooled their blending and ageing know-how into one company. Its aged rum, English Harbour, came much later and is named for the sheltered naval port on the island's south coast, where the Royal Navy kept its Caribbean dockyard and a young Horatio Nelson was stationed. The restored Nelson's Dockyard is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the distillery's older Cavalier rum remains a fixture on the island.
cachaca-envelhecida: Cachaça has been distilled from fresh cane juice in Brazil since the sixteenth century, when Portuguese settlers set up the first sugar mills on the coast. Ageing it in wood came later and was long informal, with producers using whatever casks or native timbers were to hand. Brazilian rules now reserve the word envelhecida for cachaça with at least half its volume aged a year or more in wood, with premium and extra premium grades above it. Native woods such as amburana help set the category apart.
tiquira: Tiquira comes from Maranhão in northern Brazil, where cassava has long been the staple root. Indigenous peoples of the region fermented cassava into drinks such as cauim well before the Portuguese arrived; distillation came with colonisation, and tiquira grew from that meeting of a native ferment and a European still. Nobody is credited with its invention, and the origin of the name is not documented. It remains a regional spirit, made mostly by small producers in Maranhão and rarely seen elsewhere in Brazil.
licor-de-jenipapo: Licor de jenipapo is a festival liqueur of Brazil's northeast, made by steeping the ripe fruit of the genipap tree in cachaça or spirit with sugar. The tree is native to tropical America, and long before the liqueur existed indigenous peoples used its unripe juice as a blue-black body paint that lasts on the skin for days. The liqueur has no recorded inventor; it is a home and small-producer tradition, closely tied to the June festivals of São João in Bahia.
enguindado: Enguindado takes its name from the guinda, the sour cherry, which is steeped in aguardiente with sugar and often cinnamon or cloves until the spirit turns deep red. It is a homemade tradition of the Chilean countryside rather than anyone's invention, and families keep their own proportions and steeping times. Cherry trees reached Chile with Spanish settlement, and steeping fruit in local aguardiente follows the pattern of other Chilean country liqueurs. It comes out on festive occasions, the September independence holidays among them.
singani: Singani has been distilled in the Bolivian highlands since the sixteenth century, when Spanish missionaries and settlers planted vines in the southern valleys to supply the silver boom at Potosí. Bolivian law now requires Muscat of Alexandria grapes and high-altitude vineyards, with Tarija the centre of production. The origin of the name is debated. The film director Steven Soderbergh met singani while filming in Bolivia, launched Singani 63 and lobbied US regulators to recognise it as a distinct spirit.
viche: Viche is the cane spirit of the Afro-Colombian communities of the Pacific coast, in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Cauca and Nariño. Its tradition was carried by the descendants of enslaved Africans brought to the region, with methods handed down within families over generations. For a long time it was sold informally and treated as contraband, until a national law recognised viche as heritage of the Black communities of the Pacific. It is also the base for steeped preparations such as arrechón, tomaseca and curao.
chirrinchi: Chirrinchi is the spirit of the Wayúu, the indigenous people of the La Guajira peninsula, whose lands straddle the border between Colombia and Venezuela. It is distilled from fermented panela or cane sugar in small home stills, a technique that reached the peninsula through colonial contact and was taken into Wayúu custom. No inventor or date is recorded. Its importance is social: chirrinchi is offered at wakes and gatherings and has a place in the customary negotiations that settle family agreements and disputes.
cocuy: Cocuy is made from Agave cocui, which grows in the dry hills of Falcón and Lara in north-western Venezuela. Peoples of the region are said to have roasted the plant long before the Spanish arrived; distilling came after contact, and the spirit grew up as a rural craft. A change in the law in the nineteen-seventies pushed artisanal cocuy underground, and only a later reform made it legal to sell again. Cocuy from Pecaya, in Falcón, holds a denomination of origin.
pajaro-azul: Pájaro azul is an aguardiente of Bolívar province in Ecuador's central highlands, made around Guaranda and Guanujo by steeping cane spirit with herbs, citrus leaves and spices. Some recipes are said to include chicken or other meat during distillation, and each producer guards its own version. The name, blue bird, has several local explanations and no settled one. It has become a fixture of the Carnaval de Guaranda, where it is poured along the parade routes.
grapa-argentina: Grappa reached Argentina with the great wave of Italian immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when millions of Italians settled in Buenos Aires and the wine provinces. Families who had made pomace brandy at home in northern Italy kept doing so in Mendoza and San Juan, distilling the skins and seeds left after winemaking. Spelled grapa locally, it has no single founder, and today it is made both by large wineries and by small producers keeping family stills going.
cana: Caña, cane spirit, has long been made in Argentina, above all from cane grown in the north-west around Tucumán, and it gave the countryside a cheap everyday spirit. It became a staple of the pulpería, the rural store and bar, and part of gaucho lore, and no single founder is credited with it. Caña also carries a folk custom shared with Paraguay: on the first of August many people take a little steeped with rue to mark the arrival of the month.
hesperidina: Hesperidina was created in Buenos Aires in 1864 by Melville Sewell Bagley, a young American from Maine who worked at the La Estrella pharmacy and experimented with bitter orange peel. Before the launch he is said to have painted the single word Hesperidina on walls around the city. When imitations followed, Bagley pressed for a trademark law, and Hesperidina is generally cited as Argentina's first registered mark. The name comes from hesperidium, the botanical term for a citrus fruit.
grappamiel: Grappamiel is grappa sweetened with honey, a Uruguayan habit that grew out of the Italian immigration of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Italian families who distilled grape pomace at home kept doing so in Uruguay, and honey softened the rough spirit through the cold, damp winters of the Río de la Plata. Nobody is credited with the first bottle; it was a household mixture long before brands took it up, and it is still a fixture of Uruguayan bars.
cana-paraguaya: Paraguay has grown sugarcane since the colonial period, and caña, the spirit distilled from it, became the country's national spirit long before anyone branded it. It was made on estates and in small rural stills, and some producers rested it in casks of native woods, which gave colour and a local spice. No founder is recorded. Paraguayans also keep the custom of caña con ruda: on the first of August a little caña steeped with rue is taken to mark the start of the month.
borgoe: Borgoe is usually said to have been introduced in 1982 to mark a century of the central sugar factory at Mariënburg, the old Dutch plantation in Commewijne, and its name is taken as a local form of the plantation's. Suriname's sugar and rum trade goes back to Dutch plantation agriculture of the seventeenth century. The rum is made by Suriname Alcoholic Beverages, which also bottles the white rum Black Cat, and Borgoe is its signature name at home and in the Netherlands.
potstill-brandy: South African brandy is dated to 19 May 1672, when an assistant cook aboard the Dutch ship De Pijl, anchored in Table Bay, distilled Cape wine into brandy. Distilling spread to the farms of the Cape, but the modern quality categories took shape in the twentieth century, when the industry set rules for pot stills and maturation in oak. Potstill brandy is the strictest, made almost entirely from copper pot-still spirit and aged at least three years, and houses such as KWV and Van Ryn's are known for it.
witblits: Witblits, Afrikaans for white lightning, descends from the copper pot stills that Dutch and Huguenot settlers brought to the Cape in the seventeenth century. As farming spread inland, farmers distilled unaged spirit from wine and grape leftovers for their own use, and the name stuck to the clear, high-strength result. Twentieth-century liquor laws made unlicensed distilling illegal for many years, but later reforms allowed licensed production, and a number of farm distilleries now make and sell it openly.
mampoer: Mampoer grew out of the same Cape pot-still tradition as witblits but moved inland with the trekboers, who distilled whatever fruit their farms gave them: peaches, apricots, plums, marula or prickly pear. The popular explanation for the name links it to Mampuru, a Pedi leader, though historians treat that as folklore rather than proven. Like witblits, it was long caught up in the restrictions on home distilling. Herman Charles Bosman's stories of the Groot Marico made mampoer a fixture of South African writing.
amarula: Amarula began in 1983, when the Southern Liqueur Company in South Africa launched a spirit distilled from fermented marula fruit; the cream liqueur followed in 1989 and soon became the brand. The marula, a wild tree of southern Africa also known as the elephant tree, gives the brand its name and its label, since elephants eat the fallen fruit, though the popular idea that the fruit intoxicates them is largely a myth. The fruit is gathered from wild trees by rural communities.
van-der-hum: Van der Hum is a Cape liqueur of brandy flavoured with naartjie peel and spices, and the earliest mention usually cited dates from 1861. How much older it is nobody knows, and the name is a puzzle: one explanation makes it Mr What's-his-name, because rival claimants could not agree who invented it, while another credits a Dutch sea captain. Naartjie is the South African word for a tangerine, and KWV is among the houses that still make it.
cape-gin: Fynbos gin is usually credited to Lorna Scott, who founded the Inverroche distillery at Still Bay on the southern Cape coast and is widely regarded as the first to make gin from fynbos, using plants from the surrounding hills and dunes. Fynbos is the shrubland of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms and the only one inside a single country. The idea spread through South Africa's craft distilling boom, and buchu and rooibos became familiar gin botanicals.
mahia: Mahia was the spirit of Morocco's Jewish communities, distilled at home and in small workshops from figs, dates or raisins and often scented with aniseed. Its name is usually glossed as water of life, and it belonged to festivals and family celebrations. No inventor or date is recorded; it was a household craft passed down through generations. When most of Morocco's Jews emigrated in the mid twentieth century, largely to Israel and France, the tradition went with them, and a handful of distillers now keep it going.
boukha: Boukha is the fig brandy of Tunisia's Jewish community, and its best-known house is Bokobsa. The family dates its distilling to 1880, when Abraham Bokobsa is said to have turned a household craft into a business near Tunis. The name is disputed: many sources trace it to a Judeo-Arabic word for vapour, from the steam rising off the still, while the Bokobsa family's own account links it to the word vodka. No one is credited with first distilling figs.
thibarine: Thibarine comes from Thibar, in the hills of northern Tunisia, where the Missionaries of Africa, known as the White Fathers, established an agricultural estate under the French protectorate at the end of the nineteenth century. The fathers planted vines and orchards, made wine, and produced a liqueur of dates and aromatic herbs macerated in grape spirit. Accounts differ on when the liqueur was first made, and no member of the order is credited with the recipe. It outlived the mission that created it.
zibib: Zibib is Egypt's anise spirit, part of the family that includes Levantine arak, Greek ouzo and Turkish rakı. The name comes from zabib, the Arabic word for raisin, since much of it was traditionally distilled from dried grapes and then flavoured with aniseed. No inventor or date is recorded; it developed within the eastern Mediterranean tradition of grape-based anise spirits. Like its relatives it is mixed with water, which turns it milky white, the effect known as the louche.
areke: Areke is the household spirit of the Ethiopian highlands, distilled from a ferment of grains such as barley, maize, sorghum or teff and usually bittered with gesho, the buckthorn leaf that also flavours the beer called tella. Families make it in simple clay stills, and a twice-distilled version, dagim areke, is stronger and clearer. No inventor or date is recorded; it is an old domestic craft, largely in the hands of women, tied to holidays, weddings and hospitality.
aragi: Aragi is the date spirit of Sudan, distilled from the fruit of the palms along the Nile, and its name is a local form of the word arak. It was a common household and village spirit before the Islamic laws of Jaafar Nimeiry's government banned alcohol in 1983 and drove it underground. No inventor or date is recorded. A 2020 reform allowed non-Muslims to drink in private, while the ban for Muslims remains, and aragi is still made at small scale, largely outside any licensing.
changaa: Chang'aa is Kenya's traditional distilled spirit, made from fermented maize, millet or sorghum in small home stills, and its name is usually glossed as kill me quickly. Home distilling is generally thought to have spread in the colonial period, when local spirits were banned and production moved into the informal economy. No inventor or date is recorded. Because unregulated batches were sometimes adulterated with methanol, Kenya legalised chang'aa under its Alcoholic Drinks Control Act of 2010, aiming to bring production into the open.
kenya-cane: Kenya Cane is the licensed cane spirit of Kenya Wine Agencies, the company the Kenyan government set up after independence to bring the import and distribution of wines and spirits under one roof, and which later began making its own. The company has not published a detailed history of the brand's launch, and no individual is credited with creating it. It became a staple of bars across the country as a legal, consistent cane spirit, and its makers have since added flavoured versions and a second cane spirit, Caribia.
waragi: Waragi is the general Ugandan name for locally distilled spirit, made from bananas, millet, cassava or sugarcane in village stills across the country. The name is commonly said to be a corruption of war gin, from the colonial era, though that etymology is folk history rather than documented fact. Unlicensed distilling was restricted under colonial rule and later brought under licensing, with licensed makers of the raw spirit, called enguli, required to sell it on to a distiller.
uganda-waragi: Uganda Waragi was first produced in 1965, when the government of newly independent Uganda set up a distillery to turn the country's village spirit into a regulated, bottled product. The Enguli Act of the same year required licensed makers of enguli, the raw local spirit, to sell it to the distillers, where it was redistilled and flavoured with juniper and other botanicals. The state's Uganda Distilleries made it for decades until the brand passed to Uganda Breweries, part of East African Breweries.
konyagi: Konyagi is usually dated to 1970, when it was introduced by Tanzania Distilleries, the company that still makes it, and within a generation it became the country's most familiar spirit. Made from cane spirit with flavourings and bottled at 35 per cent, it sits between gin and vodka without being either, and Tanzanians simply call it konyagi as if it were a category of its own. Its makers have not explained the name. Tanzania Distilleries is now part of the Tanzania Breweries group.
gongo: Gongo is the general Tanzanian name for village-distilled spirit, made from maize, millet, sugarcane or bananas, depending on the region, in improvised stills. It has no recorded inventor or start date; distilling spread informally and stayed outside the law, since unlicensed production is illegal in Tanzania. The name and the base ingredient change from place to place. Governments have alternated between crackdowns and proposals to license and regulate small producers, as neighbouring Kenya did with chang'aa, and the debate continues.
ogogoro: Ogogoro is distilled from palm wine, the fermented sap of raffia and oil palms, and is most closely associated with the Niger Delta, where it was made in home stills. The British colonial authorities banned local distilling, partly to protect revenue from imported gin, and labelled ogogoro illicit gin; made in secret, it became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule. Production became legal after independence, though much of it is still made informally, and new commercial bottlings now present it as a serious spirit.
akpeteshie: Akpeteshie took hold in the 1930s in what was then the Gold Coast, when the colonial government had banned local distilling and raised duties on imported spirits. Ghanaians distilled palm wine and sugarcane in secret, and the Ga name, usually explained as they are hiding, recalls that clandestine trade. The spirit became bound up with the independence movement and was legalised after independence. It is still poured on the ground as a libation to the ancestors at ceremonies.
odontol: Odontol is the name used in Cameroon for home-distilled spirit, made from palm wine, maize or sugarcane in improvised stills, and known in different regions by other names, arki among them. It has no recorded inventor or start date; like neighbouring West African palm spirits it grew up outside the licensed trade, and most of it is still made that way. The origin of the word odontol is not documented. The Cameroonian authorities have tried several times to regulate or suppress production, but village distilling has stayed widespread.
lotoko: Lotoko is the home-distilled spirit of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, made from fermented maize or cassava in stills improvised from oil drums and salvaged pipe. No inventor or date is recorded, and the origin of the name is not documented. It is produced and sold largely outside any licensing, and the authorities have periodically tried to ban it, but it is still widely made.
caporroto: Caporroto is the artisanal cane spirit of Angola, distilled by smallholders in the interior from sugarcane grown on family plots. Sugarcane came to Angola with Portuguese colonisation, and caporroto grew up beside the plantation trade as the small farmer's product rather than the estate's. Its exact beginnings, and the source of its name, are not documented, and it is rarely bottled for sale outside the country. It is mostly made and drunk locally, often at family and village occasions.
nipa: Nipa is the name used in parts of Mozambique for spirit distilled from fermented cashew apples. The cashew tree was brought to East Africa from Brazil by the Portuguese, and Mozambique became a major grower; the fleshy apple attached to each nut spoils within days, so fermenting and distilling it is one of the few ways to use it. No inventor or date is recorded, and how nipa got its name is not documented. It is made in small home stills and sold mostly locally.
grogue: Grogue is Cape Verde's cane spirit, and the islands' cane distilling is among the oldest in the Atlantic. Portugal planted sugarcane on the archipelago soon after settling it in the fifteenth century, and cane spirit, then simply called aguardente, followed. The name grogue is generally traced to the English word grog. Today most of it comes from Santo Antão and Santiago, where cane grown on steep terraces is crushed in trapiches and distilled in small copper stills.
ponche-caboverdiano: Ponche is Cape Verde's sweet companion to grogue, made by mixing the cane spirit with mel de cana, a thick syrup boiled down from sugarcane juice, and usually lime. It grew out of the same trapiche culture on Santo Antão and Santiago, where syrup and spirit come from the same cane harvest. No inventor or date is recorded, and families and small producers keep their own recipes. Despite the name, mel de cana has nothing to do with bees; it is simply cane juice cooked down.
malagasy-rhum: Sugarcane has long been grown on Madagascar, and rum distilling grew with the colonial sugar industry, centred in the north-west and on the island of Nosy Be. The best-known Malagasy brand, Dzama, is credited to Lucien Fohine, who began with a distillery beside the sugar works on Nosy Be and built a range around the island's produce. Madagascar also grows most of the world's vanilla, so vanilla rums and the household rhum arrangé follow naturally from what grows there.
toaka-gasy: Toaka gasy, simply Malagasy alcohol, is the island's village spirit, distilled from fermented cane juice or sometimes rice in small home stills, mostly in the highlands and countryside. No inventor or date is recorded; it is a household craft that has been made for generations. Production has been prohibited or restricted at various times since the colonial era, largely to protect tax revenue from licensed distilleries, and most of it is still made and sold informally, from village to village.
rhum-arrange: Rhum arrangé, arranged rum, is a household tradition of the French-speaking Indian Ocean islands, above all Réunion and Madagascar. Local rum is steeped with fruit, spices, vanilla or herbs and left for months. Nobody invented it; it grew from the rum of the islands' sugar estates and the fruit and spice that grow around them, and every family and bar keeps its own recipes. On Réunion the big jars sit on bar counters in plain view, and some distilleries now bottle their own versions.
takamaka: Takamaka rum dates from 2002, when the brothers Richard and Bernard d'Offay founded the Trois Frères Distillery on Mahé. The distillery now works from La Plaine St André, an old plantation estate from the French colonial era. The brand takes its name from the takamaka tree, a coastal tree of the Indian Ocean that shades Seychelles beaches and was traditionally used for boat-building, and it has become the islands' best-known rum.
kachasu: Kachasu is the home-distilled maize spirit of Zambia and Zimbabwe, made from fermented maize meal, sometimes with sugar or other grains, in improvised stills. It grew up in townships and villages during the colonial period, when Africans' access to European liquor was restricted, and it has stayed largely outside the law. No inventor or date is recorded. A related home brew, skokiaan, gave its title to a tune by the Zimbabwean bandleader August Musarurwa that became an international hit, recorded by Louis Armstrong among others.
ombike: Ombike is a traditional distilled spirit of the Owambo people of northern Namibia, made from fermented marula fruit, makalani palm fruit, wild berries or grain in stills of clay and salvaged metal. It is household production, largely in the hands of women, and no inventor or date is recorded. The spirit has survived colonial restrictions and periods of prohibition and is still made in villages across the north. The origin of the word is not documented, and it is rarely sold beyond local markets.
israeli-single-malt: Israeli single malt is a young category. One of its pioneers is Milk & Honey, founded in 2012 by a group of entrepreneurs in Tel Aviv, with the Scottish whisky consultant Jim Swan advising on production; its first single malt followed a few years later. The hot, humid coastal climate pushes spirit into wood quickly, and the distillery has also matured casks elsewhere in Israel, including near the Dead Sea. Other distilleries have since joined it.
sabra: Sabra was launched in 1963 and is usually credited to Edgar Bronfman Sr. of Seagram, who wanted an identifiably Israeli liqueur. The name is the Hebrew word for the prickly pear cactus, used affectionately for native-born Israelis, and the first version is said to have been flavoured with the cactus fruit. It did not catch on, and the recipe was changed to bitter chocolate and Jaffa orange, the combination that stuck. The bottle is modelled on an ancient Phoenician flask.
aragh-sagi: Aragh is the Persian word for distilled spirit, related to arak, and Iran's grape culture is among the oldest anywhere: jars from Hajji Firuz Tepe in the Zagros mountains hold wine residue some seven thousand years old. Aragh sagi, dog's sweat, is the slang name for the raisin spirit distilled at home in secret since the Islamic Revolution banned alcohol for Muslims. No inventor or date is recorded, and recognised religious minorities may make alcohol for their own use.
indian-molasses-whisky: Most whisky sold in India belongs to a category shaped by colonial and post-independence excise law: Indian-made foreign liquor, spirits made in India in the style of imported ones. With molasses plentiful and cheap from the sugar industry, distillers built their whiskies on neutral molasses spirit, blended with flavourings and sometimes a share of malt. No single founder is credited. Because European rules define whisky as a grain spirit, most of these brands cannot be sold as whisky there, though several rank among the world's largest whisky brands by volume.
coconut-feni: Coconut feni is the older of Goa's two fenis. Toddy, the sap tapped from coconut palms, is generally thought to have been fermented and distilled on the Konkan coast before the Portuguese arrived, while cashew trees came only with them, from Brazil, in the sixteenth century. The name is usually traced to the Konkani word for froth. No inventor is recorded. Coconut feni has grown rare as the number of toddy tappers has fallen, and cashew feni now dominates.
mahua: Mahua spirit is distilled from the fleshy flowers of the mahua tree, Madhuca longifolia, which fall in spring and are gathered by Adivasi communities across central India. The flowers have been fermented and distilled for generations, and the tradition has no recorded inventor. Colonial excise laws restricted village distilling, and mahua was long classed as cheap country liquor. More recently Madhya Pradesh has recognised it as heritage liquor, and new brands bottle it for wider sale.
indian-rum: Rum has been made from Indian molasses since the colonial era, when breweries and distilleries were set up to supply British troops. Its defining brand, Old Monk, came from Mohan Meakin, the company that grew out of a brewery Edward Dyer founded at Kasauli in the Himalayan foothills. Old Monk was launched in 1954, and its creation is credited to Ved Rattan Mohan, said to have been inspired by Benedictine monks. The company famously never advertised it, relying on word of mouth.
tharra: Tharra is the slang name across northern India, particularly in Punjab and the Hindi-speaking plains, for cheap country liquor, much of it distilled in villages from fermented sugarcane juice, jaggery or molasses. It has no recorded inventor or start date; it grew from long-standing rural distilling and from the colonial excise system that separated licensed country liquor from illicit production. Much of the illicit trade remains unregulated, and methanol-adulterated batches have caused repeated mass poisonings, which keeps it a constant concern for state excise authorities.
indian-gin: India's ties to gin go back to the British Raj, when officers mixed it with quinine tonic, but the country's own craft gin is usually dated to 2017, when Nao Spirits, founded by Anand Virmani and Vaibhav Singh, released Greater Than from a small distillery in Goa. Nao followed with Hapusa, from the Sanskrit word for juniper, and others such as Stranger & Sons joined them, building recipes on Indian botanicals that most gin distillers elsewhere have to import.
ceylon-arrack: Coconut arrack has been distilled in Sri Lanka for centuries from toddy, the fermented sap of coconut flowers, and it was already an export when the Dutch East India Company controlled the island's coast. Under British rule production was licensed and taxed, and in the twentieth century a few large distillers came to dominate. Toddy tappers still work the palm crowns by hand, often moving between trees on ropes strung high above the ground. The spirit is matured in vats of halmilla, a native timber.
kasippu: Kasippu is the Sri Lankan name for illicit home-distilled spirit, made in rural stills from sugar, jaggery, fermented fruit or other starches, often hidden away in jungle or paddy country. It has no recorded inventor or start date; it grew up as the unlicensed counterpart to the island's licensed arrack trade, cheaper because it escapes excise duty. Police and excise officers run regular raids, and the trade remains a revenue and safety concern.
raksi: Raksi is the home-distilled spirit of Nepal's hills, made from fermented millet or rice and, in some places, wheat or maize. It is distilled in a traditional stacked still: a pot of ferment below, a vessel inside to catch the spirit, and a bowl of cold water on top that is changed as it warms. No inventor or date is recorded; raksi belongs to a wider Himalayan tradition of grain spirits, made by many communities for festivals, rites and hospitality.
aila: Aila is the rice spirit of the Newar people of the Kathmandu valley, distilled at home from fermented rice or other grains and woven into Newar ritual life, from feasts to offerings to deities. It belongs to the wider Himalayan family of grain spirits, and it is traditionally poured from an anti, a long-spouted jug, held high above a small clay bowl. No inventor or date is recorded. Some licensed producers now bottle aila commercially, carrying it from household courtyards into restaurants.
ara: Ara is Bhutan's home-distilled spirit, made from rice, maize, millet, wheat or barley according to what each valley grows. It is a domestic craft, largely in the hands of women, offered to guests and used in religious offerings, festivals and family occasions. No inventor or date is recorded; it shares roots with the grain spirits of Tibet and the eastern Himalaya. Because Bhutan restricts the commercial production and sale of home-made ara, nearly all of it is made for the household and for visitors rather than for market.
murree: Murree began in 1860 as a brewery founded by the British near Murree, a hill station in the Punjab high and cool enough for brewing before refrigeration. Under Henry Whymper it became one of the leading breweries in British India, and production later moved down to Rawalpindi, where it remains. Since Partition the Parsi Bhandara family has controlled the company, which brews beer and distils whisky, vodka and brandy, sold legally in Pakistan to non-Muslims and foreigners.
bangla-mod: Bangla mod, Bengali for country liquor, is the cheap molasses spirit sold under licence in Bangladesh. Its licensed supply comes from Carew & Co, a distillery at Darsana in Chuadanga that began under British rule, was nationalised after independence and now sits inside a state-owned sugar mill. Licensed country liquor shops operate under an excise system inherited from colonial administration, and buyers need a permit. No individual is credited with the drink, and village distilling continues alongside the legal supply.
uzbek-konyak: Grapes have been grown in the Ferghana valley and around Samarkand since antiquity, but Uzbek brandy is a product of the Russian and Soviet era. Russian merchants built wineries in Samarkand in the nineteenth century, and Soviet planners later expanded vineyards and wine combines across Central Asia, where brandy was made in the style of Armenian and Georgian konyak, softer and sweeter than French cognac. No single founder is credited with Uzbek konyak. The Soviet word stuck, and it remains the everyday name for local brandy.
sauce-aroma-baijiu: Sauce-aroma baijiu is the style of Maotai, a town on the Chishui river in Guizhou, where sorghum spirit was being made under the Qing dynasty in workshops that later merged into Kweichow Moutai. Its name, jiangxiang, comes from an aroma that recalls soy sauce. The method follows the seasons: sorghum is fermented through a year-long cycle with two additions of grain, nine steamings, eight fermentations and seven distillations, and the spirit then rests for years before blending. Moutai's place at state banquets made it China's most famous spirit.
strong-aroma-baijiu: Strong-aroma baijiu traces its lineage to Luzhou in Sichuan, where the oldest working fermentation pits of Luzhou Laojiao are dated to 1573, in the Ming dynasty, and have been in use ever since. The style, nongxiang, is defined by those mud pits: grain ferments in them for weeks, and the microbial life built up in the clay shapes the spirit's fruity, pungent aroma. Wuliangye, from nearby Yibin, is the style's other great name, and strong aroma is now China's most widely made baijiu.
light-aroma-baijiu: Light-aroma baijiu is the style of Fenjiu, from Xinghua village near Fenyang in Shanxi, where alcoholic drinks are recorded long before distillation. Xinghua, apricot blossom village, is often linked to a famous Tang poem by Du Mu, though scholars dispute which village the poet meant. The qingxiang method ferments sorghum in buried earthenware jars rather than mud pits, which keeps the spirit clean and floral. Light aroma remains widespread in northern China, where erguotou belongs to the same family.
rice-aroma-baijiu: Rice-aroma baijiu, mixiang, is the southern Chinese style distilled from rice rather than sorghum, with Guangxi and Guangdong as its heartland. Its most famous example is Sanhua jiu from Guilin, whose makers age the spirit in caves in the karst hills around the city, including Elephant Trunk Hill. Rice distilling in the south is old and largely undocumented, and no single founder is credited. The style was named one of the four classic baijiu aromas in the twentieth century, alongside sauce, strong and light.
erguotou: Erguotou is credited to three brothers of the Zhao family at the Yuanshenghao distillery in Beijing in 1680, under the Kangxi emperor. The usual story is that they kept only the spirit that ran while the second pot of cooling water sat atop the still, which gave the style its name, second pot head. Many Beijing distilleries made it, and in 1949 a dozen were merged into a state company whose erguotou was named Red Star in honour of the new republic.
mei-kuei-lu-chiew: Mei kuei lu chiew, rose dew liquor, is a baijiu flavoured with rose petals and rock sugar, part of a long Chinese tradition of scenting spirit with flowers. Its exact origins are not documented, and no single maker is credited with it. Cantonese cooks made it a kitchen staple: it is a standard seasoning in marinades for char siu and other roast meats. Export bottlings made it a fixture of Chinese grocery shelves around the world.
yaojiu: Yaojiu, medicinal wine, belongs to a tradition as old as Chinese pharmacy: steeping roots, herbs, fungi or animal products in alcohol. Classical materia medica texts list such preparations, and the Ming physician Li Shizhen recorded many in his great compendium. There is no single origin or inventor. Modern yaojiu is usually made on a baijiu base, sold both by herbal pharmacies and by commercial brands, and ranges from ginseng infusions to snake wine, in which a whole snake is submerged in the spirit.
kaoliang: Kinmen Kaoliang Liquor was founded in 1952, a few years after the Battle of Guningtou, when General Hu Lien, commanding the island's garrison, wanted to stop shipping liquor for the troops from Taiwan. He enlisted the private distiller Ye Hua-cheng to help set up a distillery and encouraged farmers to grow sorghum, kaoliang, by trading rice for it pound for pound. The spirit took the grain's name, and the distillery became the island's main industry.
imo-shochu: Imo shochu goes back to 1705, when Maeda Riemon, a fisherman from southern Satsuma, brought sweet potatoes home from the Ryukyu Kingdom. The crop thrived in Kagoshima's thin volcanic soil, where rice did poorly, and distillers turned it into shochu. Shochu was already known there: carpenters' graffiti from 1559 in the rafters of Koriyama Hachiman shrine in Isa complains that they were never offered any, the oldest written use of the word. Kagoshima remains the style's heartland.
mugi-shochu: Barley shochu has two homes. Iki island, in Nagasaki, claims to have made it since the sixteenth century, using barley with rice koji, and holds a protected geographical indication. The light modern style came from Oita: in 1973 the Nikaido distillery released the first shochu made entirely from barley, barley koji included, and in 1979 Sanwa Shurui launched iichiko, which set off a national shochu boom. Oita has been known as Japan's barley shochu kingdom ever since, and its fruity, lightly nutty style is how many people first meet shochu.
kome-shochu: Rice shochu is most closely tied to the Hitoyoshi basin in Kumamoto, where makers along the Kuma river trace their craft back some five centuries. The basin, ringed by mountains and ruled for centuries by the Sagara clan, kept its rice-based tradition largely intact. Kuma shochu was among the first Japanese spirits to receive a geographical indication, alongside Iki shochu and Ryukyu awamori. Around two dozen small distilleries still work in the basin.
kokuto-shochu: Kokuto shochu took its legal form in 1953, when the Amami Islands returned to Japan after years of US military administration. During the war and occupation rice was scarce, and island distillers turned to the brown sugar the islands produced. Japan's liquor tax would have treated a sugar spirit as something closer to rum, so the government added a special provision allowing brown sugar shochu, made with rice koji, only in the Amami Islands. That exclusive right still stands.
japanese-gin: The modern Japanese gin category is usually dated to 2016, when the Kyoto Distillery, Japan's first dedicated gin distillery, released Ki No Bi that October. It was built on a rice spirit base with local botanicals such as yuzu, hinoki wood, bamboo leaf, sansho and gyokuro tea, split into six groups that are each distilled separately before blending. Large producers soon followed, with Suntory's Roku and Nikka's Coffey Gin among the first, and whisky and shochu distilleries began adding gins of their own.
andong-soju: Distilled soju came to Korea with the Mongols in the thirteenth century, when the Yuan empire, which had learned distilling from the Persian world, invaded the peninsula and is said to have kept a supply base at Andong. The technique took root in the households of the local gentry, who distilled rice spirit from their own grain and nuruk. Andong's version survived as a family tradition, including through bans on home distilling, and was later designated a cultural property, kept alive by master distillers such as Jo Ok-hwa.
insamju: Insamju, ginseng liquor, comes from Korea's long relationship with ginseng, which was gathered wild in the peninsula's mountains for centuries before cultivation spread, especially around Geumsan and Punggi. Steeping whole roots in distilled soju is an old household practice rather than an invention anyone is credited with, and bottles with a root visible inside became a familiar gift. Roots shaped like a human figure are especially prized, and commercial insamju is now made by several producers.
korean-whisky: Korea long drank imported and blended Scotch, and its own single malt distilling is very young. Three Societies, now known as Ki One Distillery, opened in 2020 in Namyangju, north-east of Seoul. Its founder, the Korean American Bryan Do, came from craft brewing and brought in the Scottish master distiller Andrew Shand. Its Ki One single malt was among the country's first, its maturation pace set by summers far hotter and winters far colder than Scotland's.
arkhi: Arkhi, sometimes called shimiin arkhi, is the milk spirit of Mongolia's herding families, distilled from fermented milk, usually cow's or yak's, and sometimes from airag, fermented mare's milk. The still is a simple wooden or metal cylinder set over the stove inside the ger, with a cold-water vessel on top and a cup suspended inside to catch the spirit. No inventor or date is recorded; milk distilling is a long-standing practice of the steppe, done in summer when milk is plentiful.
arak-bali: Arak Bali is distilled in village compounds across Bali from palm sap, coconut toddy or fermented rice, a craft passed down in families, notably in Karangasem in the east of the island. It plays a part in Balinese Hindu ceremony, where arak is offered alongside brem rice wine, which is one reason it was never fully suppressed. No inventor or date is recorded. For decades it sat in a legal grey area, until a provincial regulation recognised traditional Balinese drinks and opened a path to licensed production and sale.
cap-tikus: Cap tikus is the palm spirit of the Minahasa people of North Sulawesi, distilled from the sap of the aren sugar palm in simple stills. Local producers say it was being made well before Indonesian independence, but no inventor or date is recorded. The name means rat brand, and nobody has documented how it came about. It has long been part of Minahasan celebrations and hospitality, and in recent years producers have begun bottling it commercially under licence, moving it out of the informal trade.
ciu: Ciu is the cane spirit of Bekonang, a village near Sukoharjo outside Solo in Central Java, where families have distilled fermented molasses in small stills for generations. The name is generally taken to come from a Chinese word for alcohol, reflecting the part Chinese traders played in Java's sugar and arrack economy. No inventor or date is recorded. Bekonang's producers are licensed to make ethanol for medical and industrial use, while much of what they make is drunk locally as ciu.
sopi: Sopi is the palm spirit of eastern Indonesia, distilled in Maluku, Flores, Timor and nearby islands from the fermented sap of lontar or aren palms. Its name is generally traced to the Dutch zoopje, a small drink of liquor, a word that arrived with the Dutch East India Company's long presence in the spice islands. No inventor or date is recorded. Sopi holds a place in customary life, offered in marriage negotiations, ceremonies and the settling of disputes, and East Nusa Tenggara has more recently promoted a regulated bottling.
lambanog: Lambanog is distilled from tuba, the fermented sap of the coconut flower, in Luzon and especially in Quezon province around Tayabas. Filipinos were fermenting palm sap before the Spanish arrived, and Spanish records call the distilled spirit vino de coco, though it is not a wine; the colonial government later taxed and controlled its production. No inventor is recorded. Tappers move between palm crowns on bamboo poles to collect the sap, and Quezon's distilleries make most of the country's lambanog.
